lessonTitle: Subfertility, Polycystic Ovary Syndrome and Menopause

blocks.text: A couple in their early thirties have tried to conceive for 14 months. She has had periods only every 45 to 90 days since her teens, and he has never had a semen analysis. The next steps are simple, inexpensive and well defined, and most couples can be placed on a diagnostic pathway within a single clinic visit. This unit follows a woman's reproductive life from the difficulty of conceiving, through the commonest cause of ovulatory failure, to the end of ovarian function.

blocks.markdown:
**Subfertility** (infertility) is failure to conceive after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse (every 2 to 3 days). About 84% of couples conceive within a year and about 92% within two years. **Earlier assessment** is justified if the woman is 36 or older, or if there is a known cause (previous pelvic infection, oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea, previous cancer treatment, known male factor). Causes are broadly: **ovulatory disorders** (polycystic ovary syndrome, hypothalamic dysfunction, hyperprolactinaemia, premature ovarian insufficiency), **tubal or uterine factors** (damage from pelvic infection or endometriosis, adhesions), **male factor** (roughly 30% of couples), and **unexplained** (about a quarter).

**Initial investigation** is organised by cause:

- **History and examination**: duration, frequency of intercourse, previous pregnancies, cycle pattern, pelvic infection, surgery, medication, smoking and alcohol, BMI (fertility is best with BMI 19 to 30), hirsutism, thyroid and breast examination.
- **Ovulation**: a cycle length with regular menses suggests ovulation; confirm with **mid-luteal progesterone** (about 7 days before the expected period: cycle length minus 7, so day 21 of a 28-day cycle). A level above about 30 nmol/L suggests ovulation (laboratories vary). Irregular cycles prompt FSH, LH, prolactin, TSH and testosterone measurements.
- **Male factor**: **semen analysis** (volume, concentration, motility, morphology) interpreted against WHO reference limits; repeat if abnormal.
- **Tubal patency**: hysterosalpingography or hysterosalpingo-contrast sonography if no co-morbidity; laparoscopy with dye test when pelvic disease is suspected.
- **General**: test for chlamydia, check rubella immunity, advise folic acid before conception, and stop smoking and limit alcohol. Treatment may include ovulation induction, intrauterine insemination, and in vitro fertilisation (IVF) with or without intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI).

blocks.title: Interpreting the initial infertility screen
blocks.prompt: A couple have had 15 months of unprotected intercourse without conception. The woman is 33, with a regular 35-day cycle. Her mid-luteal progesterone was measured on day 21 and was 6 nmol/L. A hysterosalpingogram shows patent tubes. Semen analysis is normal. How should the progesterone be interpreted and what is the plan?

steps.text: Check the timing: in a 35-day cycle ovulation occurs about day 21, so the mid-luteal sample should be taken about 7 days before the next period, on day 28. A day 21 sample is taken too early in the luteal phase and cannot be used to judge ovulation.
Repeat the progesterone on day 28 (7 days before expected menses) to avoid a false conclusion of anovulation. The other tests (normal semen, patent tubes) exclude male and tubal factors.

Plan: if the repeat level is above about 30 nmol/L, ovulation is occurring and the infertility is unexplained, so continue to try or consider IUI or IVF per NICE criteria; if low, work up ovulatory disorders (PCOS, TSH, prolactin) and offer ovulation induction.

blocks.answer: The day 21 result is uninterpretable in a 35-day cycle; repeat on about day 28, with the remainder of the screen normal.

blocks.markdown:
**Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)** is the commonest endocrine cause of anovulatory subfertility (about 1 in 10 women). Diagnosis uses the **Rotterdam criteria**: at least two of (1) oligo- or anovulation, (2) clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne, raised free androgen index), and (3) polycystic ovaries on ultrasound (many small follicles; recent guidelines also allow raised anti-Mullerian hormone in adults), after **excluding other causes** such as thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia and non-classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia. The mechanism involves excess ovarian androgen production, disordered LH to FSH signalling and **insulin resistance** (hyperinsulinaemia drives ovarian androgen output and lowers sex-hormone binding globulin).

**Consequences** extend beyond fertility: **endometrial hyperplasia and cancer** (infrequent periods with unopposed oestrogen), insulin resistance, impaired glucose tolerance and type 2 diabetes, obesity, dyslipidaemia, obstructive sleep apnoea, depression and anxiety, and pregnancy complications (gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia). **Management** is individualised: lifestyle change and weight loss; for cycle control and hirsutism a combined hormonal contraceptive; for fewer than about 3 to 4 bleeds a year, a cyclical progestogen to induce withdrawal bleeds protects the endometrium; metformin for metabolic features; and for ovulation induction in women wishing to conceive, letrozole (or clomifene) with monitoring for multiple pregnancy; IVF is a later option with risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.

rows: Anovulation with hyperandrogenism and insulin resistance
Loss of ovarian follicles with falling oestradiol and rising FSH
Average age about 51 years in the UK (final period)
Unopposed oestrogen if HRT lacks progestogen
Type 2 diabetes, endometrial cancer, cardiovascular risk

blocks.markdown:
**Menopause** is the permanent cessation of menstruation due to loss of ovarian follicular activity, confirmed retrospectively after 12 months of amenorrhoea. The **perimenopause** is the transition with irregular cycles and fluctuating hormones. Symptoms: **vasomotor** (hot flushes, night sweats), sleep disturbance, mood change, and genitourinary syndrome of the menopause (vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, urinary symptoms). Long-term consequences include accelerated bone loss and cardiovascular risk. Menopause before 40 is **premature ovarian insufficiency**.

**Menopausal hormone therapy (HRT)** replaces oestrogen. **Women with a uterus must also receive a progestogen** to protect the endometrium from hyperplasia and cancer; women without a uterus can use oestrogen alone. Regimens: **sequential** (cyclical progestogen, producing withdrawal bleeds) in perimenopause, or **continuous combined** (no bleeding) once more than a year after the last period. Routes: oral or **transdermal** (patch or gel). Local vaginal oestrogen treats urogenital symptoms with minimal systemic absorption.

**Benefits**: the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms, improves vaginal atrophy, mood and sleep, and prevents bone loss and fracture. **Risks** depend on the type and duration of use and the woman's baseline risk: a small increase in **breast cancer** risk with combined HRT (less clear with oestrogen-only), increased **venous thromboembolism** with oral oestrogen (transdermal at standard doses does not appear to carry the same increase), a small increase in stroke with oral therapy, and endometrial cancer with unopposed oestrogen. For women starting before 60 years or within 10 years of menopause, benefits generally outweigh risks. Contraindications include current breast cancer, undiagnosed vaginal bleeding and active VTE or arterial disease (follow NICE NG23 and local guidance).

blocks.title: Choosing a hormone therapy regimen
blocks.prompt: A 51-year-old woman with an intact uterus has severe night sweats. Her last period was 14 months ago. She has a BMI of 34 and no personal history of breast cancer or thromboembolism. Choose a regimen and justify it.

steps.text: Does she need a progestogen? She has a uterus, so oestrogen alone would risk endometrial hyperplasia and cancer; a progestogen is required.

Sequential or continuous? Her last period was more than 12 months ago, so she is postmenopausal; continuous combined therapy avoids monthly bleeds. Sequential regimens are used if still perimenopausal.

Which route? A BMI of 34 raises venous thromboembolism risk. Transdermal oestrogen does not appear to raise VTE risk the way oral oestrogen does, so a patch or gel combined with a progestogen (for example the LNG-IUS or an oral progestogen) is preferable. Discuss breast cancer risk, review at 3 months, and then yearly.

blocks.answer: Continuous combined HRT using transdermal oestrogen with a progestogen, with counselling about benefits and risks and review.

items: Investigate subfertility after 12 months, or earlier if the woman is 36 or older or a cause is known.
The initial tests are semen analysis, mid-luteal progesterone, tubal patency and chlamydia screen, with a BMI and lifestyle review.
PCOS is diagnosed by two of three Rotterdam criteria after excluding other causes.
PCOS increases the risks of endometrial hyperplasia, type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
HRT in a woman with a uterus requires a progestogen.

blocks.title: Time the progesterone from the next period, not the last
blocks.text: Mid-luteal progesterone is sampled about 7 days before the expected period. In a 35-day cycle that is about day 28, not day 21. Sampling at the wrong time is a classic cause of a false diagnosis of anovulation.

points: Subfertility investigation includes history, semen analysis, confirmation of ovulation, tubal patency, chlamydia screen and lifestyle review.
PCOS (Rotterdam criteria) causes anovulatory subfertility and metabolic and endometrial risks, managed by lifestyle, cycle control, metformin and ovulation induction.
HRT is effective for menopausal symptoms and bone protection; it requires a progestogen in women with a uterus, with breast cancer and VTE risks dependent on type, route and duration.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman has been trying to conceive with her partner for 5 months with regular unprotected intercourse. Which is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Offer earlier investigation, because the woman is over 36, rather than waiting a full 12 months
Wait a further 7 months, since 12 months is always required
Start IVF immediately without any investigation
Advise that conception is impossible at this age

questions.correctOptionText: Offer earlier investigation, because the woman is over 36, rather than waiting a full 12 months

distractorRationale.a: Correct: age 36 or over justifies earlier assessment because fertility declines with age.
distractorRationale.b: The 12-month rule has exceptions, including maternal age over 36.
distractorRationale.d: Fertility declines but conception remains possible.

questions.explanation: Female fertility declines with age, and delay reduces the time available for treatment. Early assessment of ovulation, semen and tubal patency identifies a treatable cause sooner.

questions.stem: A couple is referred after 13 months of failure to conceive. The woman has regular 28-day cycles and no medical history. Which set of first-line investigations is most appropriate?

options.text: Semen analysis, mid-luteal progesterone, chlamydia screen and assessment of tubal patency
Laparoscopy and hysteroscopy for every couple
Pelvic MRI and testicular biopsy
Endometrial biopsy and CA-125

questions.correctOptionText: Semen analysis, mid-luteal progesterone, chlamydia screen and assessment of tubal patency

distractorRationale.a: Correct: these cover male factor, ovulation and tubal factor.
distractorRationale.b: Laparoscopy is invasive and reserved for suspected pelvic disease.
distractorRationale.c: MRI and testicular biopsy are not first-line.
distractorRationale.d: These tests do not address common causes of subfertility.

questions.explanation: Initial work-up looks for male factor, ovulatory failure and tubal damage with the least invasive tests. Invasive procedures are used only when the history suggests pelvic pathology.

questions.stem: A woman has a regular 32-day menstrual cycle. Using the rule that mid-luteal progesterone is sampled 7 days before the expected next period (cycle length minus 7), on which day of her cycle should it be measured?
questions.explanation: The sampling day is the cycle length minus 7, so 32 - 7 = day 25. In a 28-day cycle the same rule gives day 21, so the timing must be adjusted for cycle length.

questions.stem: A semen sample has a volume of 3.2 mL, a concentration of 20 million sperm per mL and 45% motility. Calculate the total motile sperm count in millions.
questions.explanation: Total sperm = 3.2 mL x 20 million/mL = 64 million. Motile sperm = 64 x 0.45 = 28.8 million. Total motile count helps decide between expectant management, intrauterine insemination and IVF or ICSI, and is interpreted against reference limits that vary by laboratory.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old has had 4 periods in the past year, hirsutism and acne. Pelvic ultrasound is normal, and prolactin, TSH and 17-hydroxyprogesterone are normal. Which statement is correct?

options.text: She meets the Rotterdam criteria for PCOS with oligo-ovulation and clinical hyperandrogenism, because two of three are present and other causes are excluded
She cannot have PCOS because the ovaries look normal on ultrasound
She has premature ovarian insufficiency
She has hyperprolactinaemia

questions.correctOptionText: She meets the Rotterdam criteria for PCOS with oligo-ovulation and clinical hyperandrogenism, because two of three are present and other causes are excluded

distractorRationale.a: Correct: two of three criteria plus exclusion of mimics suffice.
distractorRationale.b: Polycystic morphology is only one of three criteria and is not mandatory.
distractorRationale.c: POI is characterised by high FSH and low oestradiol and is not suggested here.

questions.explanation: PCOS is diagnosed by any two of oligo-anovulation, hyperandrogenism and polycystic ovaries after exclusion of thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia and non-classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Ovarian morphology is not required when the other two criteria are met.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old with PCOS has had only 2 periods in 12 months and is not trying to conceive. Which long-term consequence is most directly addressed by inducing regular withdrawal bleeds with a cyclical progestogen or a combined hormonal contraceptive?

options.text: Endometrial hyperplasia and cancer from unopposed oestrogen
Type 2 diabetes
Osteoporosis
Obstructive sleep apnoea

questions.correctOptionText: Endometrial hyperplasia and cancer from unopposed oestrogen

distractorRationale.a: Correct: anovulation leaves the endometrium exposed to oestrogen without progesterone, and regular shedding or progestogen reduces hyperplasia risk.
distractorRationale.b: Diabetes risk is addressed by lifestyle measures and metformin, not by inducing bleeds.
distractorRationale.c: Withdrawal bleeds do not treat osteoporosis, and PCOS is not a typical osteoporosis cause.
distractorRationale.d: Sleep apnoea is related to obesity and is not changed by withdrawal bleeds.

questions.explanation: Without ovulation, no corpus luteum produces progesterone, so the endometrium is continually stimulated by oestrogen and can become hyperplastic. Inducing regular withdrawal bleeds or delivering progestogen protects the endometrium.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman who has had a hysterectomy for fibroids requests treatment for hot flushes. Which hormone therapy is appropriate?

options.text: Oestrogen alone, because she has no uterus and does not need endometrial protection
Combined oestrogen and progestogen, because progestogen is needed in all women
Progestogen alone
No treatment is effective for hot flushes

questions.correctOptionText: Oestrogen alone, because she has no uterus and does not need endometrial protection

distractorRationale.a: Correct: progestogen is added only to protect the endometrium; without a uterus it is unnecessary and adds breast risk.
distractorRationale.c: Progestogen alone is not the most effective option for vasomotor symptoms.
distractorRationale.d: HRT is the most effective treatment.

questions.explanation: The role of progestogen in HRT is to prevent oestrogen-induced endometrial hyperplasia. After hysterectomy this risk is absent, so oestrogen alone is used, which also avoids the progestogen contribution to breast risk.

questions.stem: True or false: standard-dose transdermal oestrogen is associated with a lower risk of venous thromboembolism than oral oestrogen.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Oral oestrogen passes through the liver first and increases hepatic synthesis of clotting factors, raising VTE risk. Transdermal oestrogen bypasses first-pass metabolism, and at standard doses is not associated with the same increase, which is why it is preferred in women with risk factors such as obesity.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman with an intact uterus asks about starting HRT for flushes and low mood. Discuss the benefits and risks, the choice of regimen, and the contraindications.
markingGuide: Benefits: relief of vasomotor symptoms, improved vaginal atrophy, sleep and mood, prevention of bone loss and fracture
Risks: small increase in breast cancer with combined HRT related to duration, VTE with oral oestrogen, small increase in stroke with oral oestrogen, endometrial cancer with unopposed oestrogen
Intact uterus requires oestrogen plus progestogen; sequential if perimenopausal, continuous combined if more than 12 months since last period
Transdermal route lowers VTE risk; vaginal oestrogen for local symptoms
Contraindications: current breast cancer, undiagnosed vaginal bleeding, active VTE or arterial disease, severe liver disease
Benefits generally outweigh risks if started under 60 or within 10 years of menopause; individualised counselling and regular review per NICE NG23
questions.explanation: HRT treats the symptoms and bone loss caused by oestrogen deficiency, and the balance of benefit and risk depends on age, time since menopause, route and personal risk factors. Progestogen protects the endometrium in women with a uterus.

questions.stem: Explain the pathophysiology of polycystic ovary syndrome and its consequences for fertility, metabolic health and endometrial health, and outline treatment for a woman wishing to conceive.
markingGuide: Pathophysiology: ovarian androgen excess, altered LH to FSH signalling, insulin resistance with hyperinsulinaemia and lowered SHBG
Anovulation leading to oligomenorrhoea and subfertility
Metabolic: insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, obesity, dyslipidaemia, sleep apnoea
Endometrial hyperplasia and cancer from unopposed oestrogen
Pregnancy risks: gestational diabetes and pre-eclampsia
Treatment for conception: lifestyle and weight loss, letrozole or clomifene ovulation induction with monitoring, metformin as adjunct, IVF if refractory (risk of OHSS and multiple pregnancy)
questions.explanation: PCOS combines hyperandrogenism with insulin resistance, causing chronic anovulation. This explains why treatment targets ovulation induction for conception, and metabolic and endometrial protection in the longer term.
